topic: Light switch: why does a toggle light switch snap, even when you push it slowly? (over-center snap action: the lever squeezes a spring-loaded plunger against a rocking copper contact bar; when the plunger tip passes the bar's pivot, the spring flips the bar onto the other side and drives the lever to its stop).
principle: The toggle lever does not move the contacts directly: it pushes a spring-loaded plunger against a copper contact bar that rocks on a rod, so the spring holds the bar on one contact; moving the lever slowly only squeezes the spring until the plunger tip passes the rod (over-center), then the stored spring energy, not the finger, flips the bar to the other side so fast that an arc has no time to form.

firstComment:
Answer: the spring 🔧

The lever doesn't touch the contacts. Its inside end holds a small spring-loaded plunger that presses on a copper bar. The bar rocks on a little rod, like a seesaw, and the spring keeps one end pressed onto a contact.

Push the lever slowly: the plunger tip slides along the bar and the spring just gets squeezed. The contacts don't move.

The moment the tip passes the rod (the "over-center" point), the spring takes over and flips the bar to the other side, and the lever jumps to its stop. Snap!

That's on purpose: the contacts open and close fast no matter how slowly you push, so there's no time for an electric arc (a spark) to form and burn them. This "quick-break" idea goes back to John Henry Holmes in 1884, and the toggle light switch was patented in 1916.

(Simplified 3D model, enlarged. Real switches vary in shape, and the wires are left out.)

Sources:
Wikipedia, Light switch (the toggle mechanism provides snap action through an over-center geometry, patented in 1916 by William J. Newton and Morris Goldberg; the actuator does not control the contacts directly but through springs and levers; turning it gradually stretches the spring, and past the center point the spring, rather than the actuator, drives the contacts with an audible snap; a compression spring presses an actuator bar into a copper contact bar that rocks on a small rod; Holmes' 1884 quick-break switch left insufficient time for an arc to form): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_switch
Wikipedia, Switch (a spring-operated tipping-point mechanism assures quick motion of the contacts regardless of how fast the user moves the control, to minimize arcing and contact damage): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switch
altText: 3D animation of a light switch. An ivory toggle lever sticks out of an ivory wall plate, pointing up, under the question Why does it snap? An orange arrow slowly pushes the lever down while the plate and the wall fade away to show a side cut through the dark gray switch body. Inside, the lever's inner end holds an orange plunger with a small steel coil spring behind it; the plunger's round tip presses on a copper bar that rocks on a steel rod. The bar's lower end rests on a silver contact. As the lever moves slowly, the spring squeezes but the bar stays put, until the plunger tip passes the rod: then the bar flips to the other side in an instant and the lever snaps down to its stop. Later the lever is pushed back up and it snaps on again, the plate fades back in and the video loops. Text on screen: Why does it snap? Inside the switch. Spring squeezes. Still on. Tip nears the middle. Snap! The spring flips it. Too fast for a spark. Snap! On again. Follow, new machine tomorrow.
